problem:
The population $P(t)$ of catfishes in a particular lake follows the logistic growth model

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.1P-0.002{P}^{2},\,P(0)=5,
$$

where $t$ is the time, measured in years. For which value of $P$ is the catfish population growing at the fastest possible rate?

feedback.problem:
The population $P(t)$of rabbits in a particular forest follows the logistic growth model

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=4P-0.002{P}^{2},\,P(0)=100,
$$

where $t$ is the time, measured in years. For which value of $P$ is the rabbit population growing at the fastest possible rate?
feedback.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{P}^{′}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

For a logistic growth model, the fastest rate of growth occurs when $P=\frac{1}{2}a.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14045108/assets/9d8f5340bba4d3c407e43f2bc64a4aa2ea986be89b8024baaa4e8ae65e96e5d5.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{dt} & =4P-0.002{P}^{2} \\  & =0.002P(2\,000-P)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=2\,000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $2\,000,$ and $P$ grows at its fastest possible rate when 

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}a=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\,000=1\,000.
$$
